content: No infants in the control group required mechanical ventilation. The average age of infants at the time of study enrollment ranged from 10 to 150 hours after birth. Five trials reported all-cause mortality, five reported morbidity (three on the use of mechanical ventilation, five on treatment failure, four on pneumothorax, and two on bronchopulmonary dysplasia). No trials reported outcomes related to growth or neurodevelopment. Subgroup analyses to evaluate the effects of gestational age and birth weight were not possible due to insufficient trials. An updated search conducted on October 1, 2021, did not identify any new trials. Infants included in the studies were diagnosed with RDS based on clinical and radiological criteria and were breathing spontaneously. They were randomized to receive either early CPAP (immediately after RDS diagnosis) or delayed CPAP (initiated upon clinical deterioration as defined by the study). The mean age at which CPAP was administered was not specified in any trial. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends CPAP for preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants in specialized or intensive care units (level 2 or 3 facilities). CPAP devices include bubble CPAP, ventilator CPAP, and Infant Flow Driver CPAP, requiring interfaces such as nasal prongs or masks, along with disposable tubing and suction catheters. Skilled health workers are essential for administering CPAP, and standardized training, supervision, and monitoring are necessary. For early versus delayed CPAP in RDS, four trials reported all-cause mortality, and four reported morbidity (including mechanical ventilation, pneumothorax, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia). No trials reported growth or neurodevelopment outcomes. Evidence suggested small benefits of early CPAP, including reduced treatment failure, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and pneumothorax, with no evidence of harm. However, there was little or no effect on mortality or intraventricular hemorrhage. Families of preterm infants undergoing CPAP or mechanical ventilation often find these therapies intimidating and express concerns about their baby’s pain and discomfort. They value understanding the medical equipment and healthcare environment and seek assistance in interacting with their baby during therapy. Studies from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) indicate that bubble CPAP is both valued and acceptable to families and healthcare workers, with evidence supporting its feasibility and low cost. Caffeine is strongly recommended for treating apnea in preterm infants, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Apnea, common in preterm infants, is inversely related to gestational age and can lead to hypoxemia and bradycardia, requiring mechanical ventilation. Methylxanthines, such as caffeine, aminophylline, and theophylline, have been used since the 1970s to manage apnea. Evidence supports a loading dose of 20 mg/kg and a maintenance dose of 5 mg/kg per day for six weeks. If caffeine is unavailable, other methylxanthines may be considered. For extubation of preterm infants born before 34 weeks’ gestation, caffeine is also recommended. Evidence suggests starting caffeine 24 hours before planned extubation or as soon as possible after unplanned extubation, continuing for six days. Moderate-certainty evidence indicates benefits, including reduced mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, failed extubation, and neurodevelopmental disability, with no evidence of harm. Methylxanthines must be dispensed by healthcare workers and are available in intravenous and oral formulations. Caffeine citrate is preferred due to its once-daily dosing and ready-to-use oral formulation. Theophylline and aminophylline, which require more frequent dosing, are more widely available in LMICs. Barriers to caffeine use in LMICs include availability and cost. Standardized training and documentation are essential for effective implementation.
